profile.address: Raccoon River Valley Trail, Ortonville, Waukee, Walnut Township, Dallas County, Iowa
profile.reading:
This is Apple's data center campus in Waukee, Iowa, a western suburb of Des Moines, sited on roughly 2,000 acres near the intersection of Hickman Road and S Avenue in Dallas County -- one of a small handful of company-owned data center campuses that support Apple's own cloud services rather than any third-party cloud or colocation business. Apple first announced the project in 2017 as a $1.3 billion investment with an initial 2020 completion target; the timeline then slipped repeatedly, with permitted completion dates pushed to August 2022 and then to August 2027 under a 2019 extension request, design work beginning in 2021, and construction on the first building not starting until March 2022. That first data center building -- 315,773 square feet -- did not become operational until October 2024, seven years after the original announcement, a gap Apple has not explained publicly beyond the scale and complexity of the build.

The operating building now supports North American users of iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music, and iMessage. Apple's public materials for the site describe room for as many as five additional data center buildings on the 2,000-acre parcel, which would bring total floor area toward roughly 1.9 million square feet if fully built out, though as of the most recent public reporting Apple has not filed for permits on any building beyond the first. Apple states company-wide that all of its data centers, this one included, run on 100 percent renewable energy, a claim it has made since April 2018, though it has not published a facility-specific breakdown of power capacity or renewable sourcing for Waukee, and no figure for the building's IT load in megawatts has been made public.

Locally, the project is documented mainly through Waukee's own economic-development agreements rather than anything Apple has published directly: the city receives roughly $500,000 per year for each completed building under its arrangement with Apple, has collected about $1.5 million to date from the single operating building, and separately received a $100 million commitment from Apple toward public infrastructure and community development, plus $4 million that helped fund Triumph Park, a 66-acre recreational site the city completed in June 2023. Those municipal payments, rather than any Apple-published capacity figure, are the clearest public measure of the facility's local economic footprint so far, and they are consistent with Apple's broader pattern in this registry of disclosing state-level or company-wide investment and sustainability commitments while keeping individual building specifications private.

[batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] Apple Inc. is a public company trading as AAPL, SEC filer CIK 0000320193, headquartered in Cupertino, California. Apples data centers are one part of a broader $500 billion four-year US investment plan the company announced in February 2025, which also covers supplier work across all 50 states, roughly 20,000 new US employees, and Apple TV+ productions in 20 states.

That announcement named data center expansion specifically in North Carolina, Iowa, Oregon, Arizona, and Nevada, and separately described a new 250,000 square foot server manufacturing facility opening in Houston, Texas in 2026, built to produce the servers that power Apple Intelligence and Private Cloud Compute, work Apple says was previously done outside the United States. Apple states that all of its data centers run on 100 percent renewable energy, a company-wide claim it has made since April 2018.

The registry here tracks 6 Apple facilities across three states, Arizona, Iowa, and Oregon, all three named in Apples 2025 expansion announcement alongside North Carolina and Nevada, which are not yet reflected among this registrys current Apple rows. Apples data center footprint is smaller and more concentrated than AWSs, Googles, or Metas in this registry, consistent with Apples data centers primarily supporting its own iCloud and Apple Intelligence services rather than a third-party cloud compute business. reading.body:
Apple's Waukee data center campus, seven years from announcement to first operational building, now hosts iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and iMessage traffic for North America from a single 315,773-square-foot structure on a 2,000-acre parcel. The operator has not published a power figure for the facility, a pattern consistent across Apple's data center portfolio, so its capacity cannot be directly compared to the 18 megawatts of published IT load across Iowa's 52 mapped facilities. The site sits on land platted for as many as five additional buildings totaling roughly 1.9 million square feet, but Apple has not filed permits for construction beyond the first.

The facility's economic footprint in Dallas County is documented through municipal agreements rather than Apple's disclosures: Waukee receives roughly $500,000 annually per completed building, has collected $1.5 million from the single operating structure, and received a $100 million community investment commitment. These figures are the clearest public measure of the campus's local significance to date. Apple states company-wide that all its data centers run on 100 percent renewable energy, but has not published facility-specific power capacity or renewable sourcing for Waukee.

The campus ranks third in Iowa by published megawatts, though this ranking reflects only the state's 2 of 52 mapped facilities that disclose power figures at all. Apple's data center footprint across Arizona, Iowa, and Oregon, named in the company's 2025 US expansion announcement, remains substantially smaller and more vertically integrated than the public cloud operators tracked in this registry. The Waukee site demonstrates Apple's pattern of making substantial long-term infrastructure commitments while treating individual facility specifications as proprietary.
